rule.title: New Firewall Rule Added In Windows Firewall Exception List For Potential Suspicious Application
rule.author: frack113

es.summary: Se agregó una regla al Windows Firewall que no bloquea el tráfico de un ejecutable ubicado en una carpeta temporal, pública o de tareas. Es un patrón frecuente de malware que se abre paso en la red.
es.what_it_detects: Eventos 2004, 2071 o 2097 del log Windows Firewall With Advanced Security en los que ApplicationPath contiene rutas como \AppData\Local\Temp\, :\Users\Public\, :\Windows\Temp\, :\Windows\Tasks\, :\PerfLogs\, :\Temp\ o :\Tmp\. Se excluyen las reglas con Action = 2 (bloqueo).
es.why_it_matters: Un atacante puede crear una excepción en el firewall para que su payload reciba conexiones entrantes o salga al exterior sin bloqueos. Así debilita las defensas del host (táctica defense impairment, técnica T1686.003 en las etiquetas de la regla).
triage_steps: Revise ApplicationPath, RuleName, Direction, LocalPorts, RemoteAddresses y Profiles del evento para saber qué tráfico se permite y desde dónde.
Identifique ModifyingApplication y ModifyingUser: netsh.exe, powershell.exe o el propio binario son más sospechosos que un instalador firmado conocido.
Busque en la creación de procesos del mismo host (+/- 15 minutos) comandos como 'netsh advfirewall firewall add rule' o New-NetFirewallRule y su proceso padre.
Obtenga el hash del ejecutable en ApplicationPath, verifique su firma y su reputación, y revise cuándo y por qué proceso se creó el archivo.
Revise las conexiones de red del ejecutable y si hay puertos en escucha que coincidan con LocalPorts.
Busque alertas previas del mismo host, del mismo usuario y del mismo hash en otros endpoints.
false_positives: Instaladores o actualizadores legítimos que se ejecutan desde %TEMP% y registran una excepción temporal (por ejemplo, clientes de colaboración o juegos).
Herramientas de TI o scripts de despliegue que copian binarios a C:\Users\Public o C:\Windows\Temp y abren puertos durante una instalación autorizada.
response_steps: Confirme con el usuario o con el equipo de TI si existía un cambio o una instalación autorizada; documente la evidencia antes de actuar.
Si no se justifica, aísle el endpoint y deshabilite la regla de firewall afectada (sin eliminarla hasta preservarla como evidencia).
Ponga el ejecutable en cuarentena, bloquee su hash en el EDR y elimine los mecanismos de persistencia relacionados.
Restablezca las credenciales de ModifyingUser si hay indicios de compromiso y revise otros hosts en busca de reglas similares.
es.severity_rationale: Nivel alto, porque abrir el firewall a binarios en rutas temporales o públicas es raro en software legítimo y suele indicar malware activo.

en.summary: A Windows Firewall rule that does not block traffic was added for an executable in a temp, public or tasks folder. Malware commonly does this to open its own network path.
en.what_it_detects: Windows Firewall With Advanced Security events 2004, 2071 or 2097 where ApplicationPath contains \AppData\Local\Temp\, :\Users\Public\, :\Windows\Temp\, :\Windows\Tasks\, :\PerfLogs\, :\Temp\ or :\Tmp\. Rules with Action = 2 (Block) are excluded.
en.why_it_matters: An attacker can add a firewall exception so the payload can accept inbound connections or reach out without being blocked. This weakens host defenses (defense impairment, tagged T1686.003).
triage_steps: Review ApplicationPath, RuleName, Direction, LocalPorts, RemoteAddresses and Profiles to see what traffic is allowed and from where.
Identify ModifyingApplication and ModifyingUser. netsh.exe, powershell.exe or the binary itself is more suspicious than a known signed installer.
Search process creation logs on the same host (+/- 15 minutes) for 'netsh advfirewall firewall add rule' or New-NetFirewallRule, and check the parent process.
Hash the executable at ApplicationPath, check its signature and reputation, and find when the file was created and which process wrote it.
Check the executable's network connections and any listening ports that match LocalPorts.
Look for earlier alerts on the same host and user, and for the same hash on other endpoints.
false_positives: Legitimate installers or updaters that run from %TEMP% and register a temporary exception, such as collaboration clients or games.
IT tools or deployment scripts that stage binaries in C:\Users\Public or C:\Windows\Temp and open ports during an authorized install.
response_steps: Ask the user or IT whether an authorized change or install took place. Record the evidence before acting.
If there is no valid reason, isolate the endpoint and disable the firewall rule. Keep it as evidence instead of deleting it.
Quarantine the executable, block its hash in EDR and remove any related persistence.
If compromise is likely, reset ModifyingUser's credentials and check other hosts for similar rules.
en.severity_rationale: High fits because legitimate software rarely opens the firewall for binaries in temp or public folders, so this usually points to active malware.

positive.description: Inbound allow rule (event 2004) added via netsh for an executable in the user's AppData\Local\Temp folder.
Outbound allow rule (event 2097) added on Windows 11 for a binary in C:\Users\Public.

negative.description: Same suspicious Temp path, but the rule blocks the application (Action 2), so the filter excludes it.
Allow rule for an application installed under Program Files, which is not a monitored location.
